title: Why You Need To Be Brutally Honest With Difficult Students ficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that false or exaggerated praise for difficult students—celebrating minimal effort as a great achievement—ultimately undermines their improvement, using an illustrative example of a teacher over-praising a student for an ordinary, unremarkable day. He identifies four harms of dishonest praise: it lowers behavioral standards, implicitly tells students they aren't capable of meeting normal expectations, teaches students to manipulate teachers for attention, and fails to produce any lasting improvement. Linsin insists teachers must reject the idea that a difficult student's current behavior is 'the best they can do,' since all students retain the capacity to change. Instead, he calls for honest assessment of where a student stands combined with a clear vision of how to improve, arguing that only praise grounded in truth carries meaning and motivates genuine growth.
points: False or exaggerated praise for difficult students undermines rather than supports lasting behavioral improvement.
Dishonest praise lowers behavioral standards, implies students can't meet normal expectations, and teaches manipulation for attention.
Reject the belief that a difficult student's current behavior represents 'the best they can do'—all students retain the capacity to change.
Give an honest assessment of where a student currently stands, paired with a clear vision for improvement.
Praise grounded in truth carries real meaning to students and motivates genuine, lasting change, unlike empty flattery.
quotes: Difficult students don’t benefit from being coddled or having smoke blown in their ears. Yet, few teachers actually tell it like it is.
It tells students that mediocre is not only good enough, but it’s celebrated. When the standard for earning praise is down around their kneecaps, what motivation do students have to go any higher?
If they can get a pat on the back from you for minimal effort, they’ll work that knowledge to get attention whenever they need it—making them feel special, haughty even, in front of their classmates.
If the thought ever enters your mind that some of your students aren’t capable of becoming well behaved, push it aside. Because it isn’t true.
A teacher’s limiting beliefs not only deeply affect students, but they also affect what the teacher is capable of.
If you’re always honest with difficult students, they’ll learn quickly that when you praise them, they can take it to the bank.
Praise based on truth will mean something to your students. Deep inside. Where real change takes place.
